'''Carol Lynn Folt''' (born 1951) is an American ecologist and academic administrator who served as the 12th president of the [[University of Southern California]] from July 2019 to June 2025. She previously served as the 11th chancellor of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] from 2013 to 2019 and as interim president of [[Dartmouth College]] from 2012 to 2013.

==Early life and education==
A native of [[Akron, Ohio]], Folt is the granddaughter of immigrants from [[Albania]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-usc-president-carol-folt-unc-20190322-story.html|title=College admissions scandal: Can USC's cautious new leader be the crusader it needs?|last1=Branson-Potts|first1=Hailey|last2=Ryan|first2=Harriet|date=March 22, 2019|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=March 23, 2019|last3=Hamilton|first3=Matt|archive-date=March 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322234325/https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-usc-president-carol-folt-unc-20190322-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> from her mother's side.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-10-09 |title=Get to Know USC President Carol L. Folt |url=https://today.usc.edu/usc-president-carol-folt-students-faculty-sustainability/ |access-date=2024-08-01 |website=USC Today |language=en-US}}</ref>

Folt attended the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], receiving a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with a major in [[aquatic biology]] in 1976 and a [[Master of Arts]] in biology in 1978.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-03-16 |title=Carol L. Folt |url=https://biology.dartmouth.edu/people/carol-l-folt |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=Department of Biological Sciences |language=en |archive-date=July 22, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240722065112/https://biology.dartmouth.edu/people/carol-l-folt |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Milestones |url=https://www.alumni.ucsb.edu/coastlines/summer-2019/milestones |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=UC Santa Barbara Alumni |language=en |archive-date=December 4, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201204173420/https://www.alumni.ucsb.edu/coastlines/summer-2019/milestones |url-status=live }}</ref> She received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in [[ecology]] from the [[University of California, Davis]] in 1982.<ref name="thesis-folt-1982">{{cite thesis |title=The effects of species interactions on the feeding and mortality of zooplankton (Tahoe) |date=1982 |institution=University of California, Davis |degree=Ph.D. |last=Folt |first=Carol Lynn |id={{ProQuest|303070520}} |oclc=983753415}}</ref> Her doctoral advisor was [[Charles R. Goldman|Charles Goldman]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Perla |first=Stephanie |date=2019-09-18 |title=2019 Award of Distinction Recipients {{!}} College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences |url=https://caes.ucdavis.edu/news/events/college-celebration/recipients/2019-award-of-distinction-recipients |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=caes.ucdavis.edu |language=en |archive-date=June 15, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240615144650/https://caes.ucdavis.edu/news/events/college-celebration/recipients/2019-award-of-distinction-recipients |url-status=live }}</ref> Folt completed postdoctoral studies at the [[Kellogg Biological Station]] of [[Michigan State University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carol Folt |url=https://www.usc.edu/profile/carol-l-folt/ |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=USC |language=en-US |archive-date=July 28, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240728220914/https://www.usc.edu/profile/carol-l-folt/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Career==
===Dartmouth College===
Folt joined Dartmouth College in 1983 as a research instructor in biological sciences and has conducted extensive research in metal toxicity. Since 2007, she has held an endowed professorship in biological sciences.<ref name="UNCannouncement">{{cite press release |title=Folt named Carolina chancellor |date=April 12, 2013 |url=http://www.unc.edu/spotlight/folt-interim-dartmouth-college-president-named-carolina-chancellor |access-date=April 13, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130415100324/http://www.unc.edu/spotlight/folt-interim-dartmouth-college-president-named-carolina-chancellor/ |archive-date=April 15, 2013 |work=UNC Press Office}}</ref><ref name="Dartmouthbio">{{cite web |title=Dartmouth biography |url=http://www.dartmouth.edu/~president/bio |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017211736/http://www.dartmouth.edu/~president/bio |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=April 13, 2013}}</ref>

Folt joined Dartmouth's administration in 2001 when she was named dean of graduate studies and associate dean of the faculty. She became dean of the faculty in 2004. She was tapped as acting provost in 2009 and appointed provost in 2010. When Dartmouth president [[Jim Yong Kim]] was named as president of the [[World Bank]] in July 2012, Folt was named acting president.<ref name=UNCannouncement/>

===University of North Carolina===
On April 14, 2014, Folt was chosen as the 11th chancellor of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] by the [[University of North Carolina Board of Governors|board of governors]] of the [[University of North Carolina|University of North Carolina System]], effective July 1, 2013. She succeeded [[Holden Thorp]], who resigned from the position in June 2013 amid allegations of widespread academic fraud.<ref name="N&O">Stancil, Jane; Blythe, Anne. [http://www.newsobserver.com/2013/04/13/2820917/carol-folt-named-as-first-female.html UNC-CH names Carol Folt first female chancellor] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130414101804/http://www.newsobserver.com/2013/04/13/2820917/carol-folt-named-as-first-female.html|date=April 14, 2013}} [[The News & Observer]], April 13, 2013.</ref>

====Academic-athletic scandal====
{{Main|University of North Carolina academic-athletic scandal}}
Under Chancellor Folt's direction, UNC spent approximately 18 million dollars defending itself from NCAA sanctions for prolonged and widespread fraud within academic and athletics departments, the details of which were outlined in Wainstein Report.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newsobserver.com/news/local/education/unc-scandal/article140688913.html|title=Cost of bills in UNC academic scandal nears $18 million|newspaper=[[The News & Observer]]|access-date=March 22, 2019|url-access=subscription|archive-date=March 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322052041/https://www.newsobserver.com/news/local/education/unc-scandal/article140688913.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/1344054-full-wainstein-report.html|title=Investigation of Irregular Classes in the Department of African and Afro-American Studies at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|date=October 16, 2014|access-date=June 24, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214154338/http://www.documentcloud.org/documents/1344054-full-wainstein-report.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Report summarizes the findings of an independent investigation conducted by former federal prosecutor Kenneth Wainstein. It describes abuses spanning over 18 years (during the tenures of Chancellor [[Michael Hooker]], Chancellor [[James Moeser]], Chancellor [[Holden Thorp]]), including "no-show" classes that had little to no faculty oversight. Approximately half of the enrollees in these "no-show" classes were athletes.

When the Wainstein Report was released in 2014, Folt acknowledged "It is just very clear that it was an academic issue with the way the courses were administered, and it is clearly an athletics issue." The [[Southern Association of Colleges and Schools]], the [[regional accreditation]] body for UNC, took the nearly unprecedented step of placing UNC on a year of probation, wherein any further missteps would lead to the university's accreditation being removed, effectively dooming the entire university. Folt brought forth reforms on several levels, and the probation was consequently lifted with no further sanctions after a year.

While not nearly as important for the well-being of the university as a whole, UNC also faced the possibility of serious sanctions from the [[NCAA]]. Under Folt's leadership, the university later went on to deny that the academic fraud was specifically benefiting athletics in its defense to the NCAA, broadly attempting to insulate the UNC administration from the findings of the Wainstein Report and the allegations of UNC whistleblower Mary Willingham. One of the university's key assertions in its defense was that the NCAA did not have jurisdiction, since the university created and offered "no-show" courses not as part of a systemic effort to benefit athletes, but the student body in general.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.dailytarheel.com/article/2017/10/a-chapter-closes-six-years-later|title=A chapter closes, six years later|newspaper=[[The Daily Tar Heel]]|access-date=March 22, 2019|first=Corey|last=Risinger|date=October 16, 2017|archive-date=March 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322052050/https://www.dailytarheel.com/article/2017/10/a-chapter-closes-six-years-later|url-status=live}}</ref> While citing the failure of multiple UNC administrators to cooperate with the investigation, the NCAA's Committee on Infractions did not hold UNC responsible, finding that "no-show" classes were not specifically designed to benefit athletes.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/unc-verdict-ncaa-ruling-sanctions-student-athlete-amateurism-fbi-probe/ |title=NCAA's 'student-athlete' hypocrisy comes full circle with North Carolina verdict |website=CBSSports.com |access-date=March 22, 2019 |first=Reid |last=Forgrave |date=October 13, 2017 |archive-date=May 1, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190501232853/https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/unc-verdict-ncaa-ruling-sanctions-student-athlete-amateurism-fbi-probe/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This finding led both fans and media across the country to question "the integrity of the NCAA, suggesting that UNC's case would open the doors for other universities to set up similar no-show classes so long as non-athletes could enroll."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wralsportsfan.com/even-within-unc-reactions-to-ncaa-s-lack-of-action-vary/17014301/|title=Folt: NCAA correct, fair; UNC whistleblowers: Not so fast|last=WRAL|date=October 13, 2017|website=WRALSportsFan.comn|access-date=March 22, 2019|archive-date=March 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322052040/https://www.wralsportsfan.com/even-within-unc-reactions-to-ncaa-s-lack-of-action-vary/17014301/|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Silent Sam monument controversy====
During her term as chancellor, Folt dealt with the controversy over the monument ''[[Silent Sam]]'', which included demonstrators outside her office.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-carol-folt-usc-president-20190320-story.html|title=USC selects Carol Folt as new president as university tries to move past scandals|last1=Ryan|first1=Harriet|last2=Hamilton|first2=Matt|date=March 20, 2019|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=March 20, 2019|archive-date=March 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190320194004/https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-carol-folt-usc-president-20190320-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Folt resigned as chancellor on January 14, 2019, effective end of the spring semester, stating: "There has been too much recent disruption due to the monument controversy". In the same letter, she ordered the remaining [[plinth]] (pedestal) to be removed, as a threat to campus safety.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.unc.edu/posts/2019/01/14/folt-resignation-orders-confederate-monument-pedestal-removed/|title=Chancellor Folt announces resignation, orders Confederate Monument pedestal to be removed intact|first=Carol|last=Folt|publisher=University Communications, [[University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill]]|date=January 14, 2019|archive-date=January 14, 2019|access-date=January 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190114233239/https://www.unc.edu/posts/2019/01/14/folt-resignation-orders-confederate-monument-pedestal-removed/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later, the [[University of North Carolina]] system board of governors made her resignation effective January 31, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2019/01/16/unc-board-moves-accept-folt-resignation-month-earlier-expected|title=UNC board moves to accept Folt resignation this month, earlier than expected|last=Seltzer|first=Rick|website=[[Inside Higher Ed]]|access-date=March 22, 2019 |date=January 16, 2019}}</ref>

===University of Southern California===
Folt became president of USC on July 1, 2019. The University of Southern California's board of trustees appointed her. She was the unanimous choice by the search committee to usher in a new era for the university following a series of high-profile scandals.<ref name="USCPresident">{{cite news |date=March 19, 2019 |title=USC selects Carol Folt as new president as university tries to move past scandals |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-carol-folt-usc-president-20190320-story.html |access-date=October 13, 2022 |work=The Los Angeles Times |language=en |archive-date=October 28, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221028201728/https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-carol-folt-usc-president-20190320-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In February 2020, Folt announced a plan to eliminate tuition for families earning $80,000 or less annually. Additionally, the university said it would no longer consider home equity in financial aid calculation.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Brown|first=Kailyn|date=2021-12-17|title=USC offers free tuition to families making under $80,000 and a break for homeowners
|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-02-20/usc-financial-aid-expansion-free-tuition-families-home-equity|access-date=2022-11-29|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

As part of Folt's reform efforts, in March 2021 the university agreed to pay more than $1.1 billion to former patients of campus gynecologist [[George Tyndall]] who was accused of preying on a generation of USC women.<ref>{{cite news |title=USC payout on gynecologist sex abuse claims to top $1 billion |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-03-25/usc-payout-gynecologist-sex-abuse-claims-to-top-1-billion |access-date=November 12, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 25, 2021 |first1=Matt |last1=Hamilton |first2=Harriet |last2=Ryan |archive-date=March 25, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210325203402/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-03-25/usc-payout-gynecologist-sex-abuse-claims-to-top-1-billion |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Anti-Zionist Tweet incident====
In the summer of 2021, USC had a free speech quagmire over tweets posted by Yasmeen Mashayekh, a 21-year-old Palestinian civil engineering student whose statements included, "I Want to Kill Every Motherfucking Zionist". On December 1, 2021, 60 faculty members sent the latest in a series of letters to USC President Carol Folt, Provost Charles Zukoski, and board of trustees' chair [[Rick Caruso]], urging the school to publicly rebuke Mashayekh and take action "to distance USC from her hateful statements."<ref name="anti-semitic">{{Cite magazine|first=Ian|last=Spiegelman|date=2021-12-17|title=USC in Free Speech Furor Over Student Who Tweeted 'I Want to Kill Every Motherf-cking Zionist'|url=https://www.lamag.com/citythinkblog/usc-in-free-speech-furor-over-student-who-tweeted-i-want-to-kill-every-motherf-cking-zionist/|access-date=2021-12-31|magazine=[[Los Angeles Magazine]]|archive-date=December 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211231022358/https://www.lamag.com/citythinkblog/usc-in-free-speech-furor-over-student-who-tweeted-i-want-to-kill-every-motherf-cking-zionist/|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Honoring Nisei Students====
In April 2022, President Folt awarded honorary degrees posthumously to 33 [[Japanese-American]] students who saw their USC educations derailed during [[World War II]] when USC, unlike other universities, refused to let its Nisei students return to study and denied them their rightful transcripts. Folt also dedicated a rock garden on the USC campus to honor the university’s Nisei students.<ref>{{cite news |title=USC gives honorary degrees to Japanese American students |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-04-02/usc-offers-posthumous-degrees-japanese-students |access-date=November 16, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=April 2, 2022 |first=Jaimie |last=Ding |archive-date=November 16, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116185508/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-04-02/usc-offers-posthumous-degrees-japanese-students |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Renaming center for public affairs====
In June 2020, Folt announced the university was stripping the name of former USC President [[Rufus Von KleinSmid]] - an active supporter of the eugenics movement - from its international center for public affairs.<ref>{{cite news |title=USC removes name of Rufus von KleinSmid, a eugenics leader, from prominent building |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-06-11/usc-removes-name-of-former-president-rufus-von-kleinsmid-a-supporter-of-eugenics-from-prominent-building |access-date=November 16, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=June 11, 2020 |first1=Teresa |last1=Watanabe |first2=Tomás |last2=Mier |archive-date=June 23, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200623131432/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2020-06-11/usc-removes-name-of-former-president-rufus-von-kleinsmid-a-supporter-of-eugenics-from-prominent-building |url-status=live }}</ref> In April 2022, Folt decided to rename the building in honor of [[Joseph Medicine Crow]], a Native American alumnus and World War II war hero.<ref>{{cite news |title=A USC building stripped of eugenicist's name will instead honor a Native American alumnus |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-11-18/usc-native-american-alumnus-building-renamed |access-date=November 16, 2022 |newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]] |date=November 18, 2021 |first=Melissa |last=Gomez |archive-date=November 16, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116191042/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-11-18/usc-native-american-alumnus-building-renamed |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Renaming track stadium field====
In 2023, Folt led the renaming of the field at the track stadium, [[Katherine B. Loker]] Stadium, at USC.<ref name="track">{{cite news |title=USC renaming its track in honor of Allyson Felix |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/usc/story/2023-01-18/usc-renaming-its-track-in-honor-of-allyson-felix |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=January 18, 2023 |access-date=June 17, 2025 |author=Helene Elliott}}</ref> The field had formerly been named Cromwell Field in honor of [[Dean Cromwell]].<ref name="track"></ref> Under Folt, USC renamed the field in honor of [[Allyson Felix]].<ref name="track"></ref>

====Cancellation of Valedictorian Speech and Commencement Speakers====
In April 2024, Folt and her administration were met with widespread controversy following her decision to restrict valedictorian Asna Tabassum from speaking during that year's commencement ceremony. USC cited safety concerns stemming from Tabassum's pro-Palestinian viewpoints. In regards to the cancellation of Tabassum's commencement speech, Folt stated that it would be "very hard" to guarantee Tabassum's safety, believing that the cancellation was a way to be "better prepared."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mecklin |first=Hali |last2=Shea |first2=Paige |last3=Albert |first3=Laya |last4=Khan |first4=Mohammed Zain Shafi |date=2025-03-05 |title=USC President Carol Folt reflects on her tenure at USC: ‘You’re not there to necessarily please people’ |url=https://www.uscannenbergmedia.com/2025/03/04/usc-president-carol-folt-reflects-on-her-tenure-at-usc-youre-not-there-to-necessarily-please-people/ |access-date=2025-10-13 |website=Annenberg Media |language=en}}</ref> Following several on-campus protests, statements from dozens of human rights organizations, and national coverage, USC further restricted all external speakers from speaking at that year's commencement.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kaleem |first1=Jaweed |last2=Orellana Hernandez |first2=Angie |last3=Hamilton |first3=Matt |date=27 April 2024 |title=13 days that rocked USC: How a derailed commencement brought 'complete disaster' |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-04-27/usc-valedictorian-commencement-turmoil |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref>

The following week, USC became embroiled in additional controversy following a pro-Palestinian protest demanding USC divestment from Israeli interests, which took place in a central plaza of campus. After involved students refused to disperse despite demands from campus police, the university brought the [[Los Angeles Police Department]] in to remove protestors. The situation escalated to involve the complete closure of all campus facilities, the campus itself, and the arrests of 93 protestors.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Orellana Hernandez |first1=Angie |last2=Kaleem |first2=Jaweed |last3=Gomez |first3=Melissa |date=24 April 2024 |title=LAPD arrests 93 people at USC amid Israel-Hamas war protests |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-04-24/usc-pro-palestinian-encampment |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |archive-date=April 28, 2024 |access-date=April 28, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240428023857/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-04-24/usc-pro-palestinian-encampment |url-status=live }}</ref> Folt, along with provost [[Andrew T. Guzman|Andrew Guzman]], were censured by USC's Academic Senate for their handling of the protest.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hubler |first=Shawn |last2=Saul |first2=Stephanie |last3=Cowan |first3=Jill |date=2024-05-09 |title=U.S.C. President Censured by Academic Senate After Weeks of Turmoil |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/08/us/university-of-southern-california-carol-folt-censure.html |access-date=2025-04-22 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> 

On April 25, 2024, Folt announced that the campus commencement ceremony in May would not take place.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kaleem |first1=Jaweed |last2=Hamilton |first2=Matt |date=25 April 2024 |title=USC cancels 'main stage' commencement ceremony |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-04-25/la-me-usc-commencement-canceled |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |archive-date=April 26, 2024 |access-date=April 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240426225451/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-04-25/la-me-usc-commencement-canceled |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Announced retirement====
On November 8, 2024, Folt announced plans to retire at the end of the 2024–2025 school year and remain on the faculty of the University of Southern California.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carol Folt to retire as president of USC at end of academic year |url=https://today.usc.edu/carol-folt-to-retire-as-president-of-usc-at-end-of-academic-year/ |date=November 8, 2024 |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=USC |archive-date=November 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241108221220/https://today.usc.edu/carol-folt-to-retire-as-president-of-usc-at-end-of-academic-year/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In February 2025, the USC Board of Trustees announced that the university's general counsel [[Beong-Soo Kim]] would succeed Folt as interim president starting on July 1, 2025.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/losangeles/news/usc-beong-soo-kim-interim-president-carol-folt-retirement/ |title=USC names General Counsel Beong-Soo Kim as interim president after Carol Folt's retirement |date=February 6, 2025 |first=Chelsea |last=Hylton |work=[[CBS News]]}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Folt is married to Dartmouth professor David Peart; they have two children.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carol Folt |url=https://www.usc.edu/profile/carol-l-folt-2/ |access-date=2024-10-28 |website=USC |language=en-US |archive-date=August 5, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240805203102/https://www.usc.edu/profile/carol-l-folt-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
